comparison: Both strongly support that macular patterning and hair cell localization are preserved in GPR156 mutants. OpenEval focuses on C5, C21-C24, C27 (striolar organization), while peer review covers C5, C21-C27 (including hair cell type distribution C25-C26). Both cite quantitative data with appropriate statistics showing no significant differences between mutants and controls.

OpenEval evaluates hair cell type distribution (C6, C25-C27) as supported by immunolabeling data. Peer review includes these claims (C25-C27) within their broader evaluation of preserved anatomical features. Both agree on the preservation of hair cell organization despite reversed polarity.

Both strongly support preservation of electrophysiological properties in mutant hair cells. OpenEval focuses on C7, C28-C31 (mechanotransduction and adaptation), while peer review covers C7, C28-C31, C33, C35, C74. Both cite comprehensive electrophysiological recordings showing normal transduction, adaptation kinetics, and voltage-activated currents.

OpenEval evaluates Type I and Type II hair cell electrophysiological properties (C32-C33) as supported. Peer review includes C33 in their broader evaluation of preserved electrophysiological features. Both agree these distinctive properties are maintained in mutants.

OpenEval rates C34-C35 as UNCERTAIN due to low statistical power for detecting subtle differences in striola and MES zones. Peer review includes C35 in their SUPPORTED evaluation of overall electrophysiological preservation. This represents a minor disagreement in confidence level regarding subtle regional differences.

Perfect agreement on zebrafish mechanosensitive calcium imaging data (C8, C40-C42, C71, C73). Both support that GPR156 loss causes all hair cells to show larger responses resembling wild-type posterior-to-anterior cells, demonstrating loss of functional asymmetry. Both treat this as convincing evidence for GPR156's role in mechanotransduction.

Both strongly support that afferent innervation patterns are preserved despite loss of hair cell orientation reversal. OpenEval focuses on C9, C44-C51 (dye-filling and genetic labeling showing maintained terminal organization). Peer review covers C9, C44-C51 plus additional claims about synaptic selectivity (C82, C90, C101-C104, C106, C108-C110, C112). Both treat this as a major finding showing orientation is not the determinant of afferent selectivity.

Both support that afferents maintain selectivity based on Emx2 expression despite altered hair cell function. OpenEval evaluates C10, C101-C104 (single fiber labeling showing similar HC contacts and high selectivity). Peer review includes C101-C104, C106, C108-C109 in their broader evaluation. Both agree this demonstrates afferent patterning uses different effectors than hair cell orientation.

Both support preservation of synaptic organization. OpenEval evaluates C105-C109 (immunolabeling showing complete synapses unchanged in gpr156 mutants vs. increased unpaired synapses in emx2 mutants). Peer review includes C106, C108-C109 in their evaluation of preserved afferent selectivity. Both agree this distinguishes gpr156 from emx2 mutants.

Both support that afferent firing properties are preserved. OpenEval evaluates C52-C54 (current-clamp recordings showing similar thresholds and firing patterns). Peer review evaluates C53-C54 as part of comprehensive electrophysiological characterization. Both agree afferent excitability is independent of hair cell orientation.

Both support that general balance and posture behaviors are preserved. OpenEval evaluates C11, C77-C79 (balance beam, tail hanging, air righting, contact inhibition all normal). Peer review includes C11, C77-C79 in their evaluation of 'mild behavioral dysfunction' with normal posture and balance. Both agree canal-driven behaviors are intact.

Perfect agreement on swimming test deficits. Both support C12, C55-C57, C87 showing significantly reduced time to rescue in mutants (17.4±2.7s vs 49.9±3.0s, p<0.0001). Both treat this as a major otolith-dependent behavioral deficit and genuine consequence of loss of hair cell polarity reversal.

Both support preservation of VOR and OKR responses. OpenEval evaluates C58-C62 (comparable gain, phase, and motor learning). Peer review includes C58-C62 in their evaluation showing 'normal balance beam, VOR and OKR.' Both agree canal-driven vestibulo-ocular reflexes are preserved.

Both support OVAR deficits as evidence of otolith-specific dysfunction. OpenEval evaluates C13, C63-C66 (preserved transient but reduced steady-state bias). Peer review evaluates C13, C64-C66, noting 'perturbed' vestibulo-ocular reflexes in OVAR. Both agree this demonstrates specific otolith dysfunction while distinguishing transient from steady-state responses.

Both strongly support the main conclusion that GPR156 mediates hair cell orientation reversal but not afferent selectivity. OpenEval evaluates C14-C16, C89 as the central finding. Peer review evaluates C14-C16, C89, C91, C99, explicitly stating this 'demonstrates that the bimodal pattern of afferent nerve projections...is not causally related to the bimodal distribution of hair-bundle orientations.' Both treat this as the major conceptual contribution.

Both support that EMX2 uses different downstream effectors for orientation versus afferent patterning. OpenEval evaluates C67, C90-C92, C112 (Advillin-positive neurons maintain segregation despite loss of orientation reversal). Peer review includes C91 in their evaluation of the bifurcation of Emx2-dependent processes downstream of Gpr156. Both agree this establishes a framework for identifying other EMX2 targets.

OpenEval evaluates C67, C90-C92, C112 regarding EMX2's bifurcated signaling. Peer review includes C90, C112 in their broader evaluation of preserved afferent selectivity. Both support that the process of Emx2-dependent synaptic selectivity bifurcates downstream of Gpr156.

OpenEval evaluates C67, C90-C92, C112 as supported evidence for bifurcated EMX2 signaling. Peer review includes C67 in their evaluation connecting preserved cellular properties to behavioral deficits. Both implicitly support the interpretation that different EMX2 effectors control different developmental processes.

OpenEval rates C72 (GPR156 affects Tmc channel function) as UNCERTAIN, noting it is speculative and based on inference rather than direct testing. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addresses this mechanistic speculation about Tmc channels.

OpenEval rates C85-C88, C94-C98 as UNCERTAIN, noting the explanations for behavioral differences between models rely heavily on speculation. Peer review includes C87 in their SUPPORTED evaluation of swimming deficits. The disagreement is about confidence in mechanistic explanations rather than the behavioral data itself.

OpenEval rates C85-C88, C94-C98 as UNCERTAIN regarding comparative behavioral phenotype explanations. Peer review includes C85 in their SUPPORTED evaluation of 'mild behavioral dysfunction.' The difference reflects OpenEval's skepticism about mechanistic speculation versus peer acceptance of the overall behavioral characterization.

Both support that Gpr156 mutants provide a cleaner model than Emx2 mutants. OpenEval evaluates C99-C100, C113 as a methodological conclusion about isolated defects. Peer review includes C99 in their evaluation that the study 'establishes a framework for the following studies.' Both agree this model enables dissection of EMX2's multiple downstream pathways.

Peer review evaluates C67, C76, C84 regarding the logic connecting preserved cellular properties to behavioral deficits. OpenEval addresses C67 in R16 but does not have a separate evaluation specifically for C76 and C84. Peer review implicitly supports this interpretive framework through acceptance of overall findings.
